chunks: Ali, from his father, from Abu Hashim al-Ja'fari who said:

We were in the presence of al-Ridha (peace be upon him) and we were discussing the intellect and good manners. So he said: 'O Abu Hashim! The intellect is a gift from God, and good manners is an effort and burden. So whoever strives to develop good manners will have ability over it; but whoever pretends to have intellect will only increase in ignorance by doing so.'

key_terms.الْأَدَب: Good manners, refinement, adab — cultivated etiquette and moral deportment, acquirable through effort
key_terms.الْعَقْل: Intellect/reason ('aql) — the divinely-gifted capacity for understanding and discernment, central to Shia theology
key_terms.تَكَلَّفَ: To strive/burden oneself with; in the second use, to feign/pretend to possess
key_terms.حِبَاء: Gift/bestowal — specifically a generous gift granted without request
key_terms.كُلْفَة: Effort, burden, something that requires striving to acquire

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Ridha say about the difference between intellect and good manners?
ai.summary: Imam al-Ridha (peace be upon him) draws a fundamental distinction between intellect ('aql) and good manners (adab): intellect is a divinely bestowed gift that cannot be acquired through effort, while good manners can be cultivated through deliberate practice. The Imam warns that feigning intellectual depth — pretending to wisdom one does not genuinely possess — only deepens one's ignorance. This teaching was addressed to Abu Hashim al-Ja'fari, a close companion, in the context of a discussion the companions themselves initiated, suggesting it arose from a practical question about self-improvement.
